title: Reflections on Trusting Trust, Revisited: Poisoning Self-Modifying AI Coding
content:
Computer Science > Cryptography and Security
  [Submitted on 15 Sep 2026]
    Title:Reflections on Trusting Trust, Revisited: Contaminating Self-Modifying AI Coding Agents with Poisoned Benchmarks
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Thompson's "Reflections on Trusting Trust" showed that a compiler can be poisoned to reinsert its own backdoor, so that even recompiling clean source reproduces the Trojan. Today, substantial coding work is done by AI coding agents -- and increasingly, those agents generate new versions of themselves. We reconsider Thompson's attack when the "compiler" is a self-modifying coding agent. Can an adversary supply poisoned benchmarks to the agent's self-evaluation and self-improvement process to induce future versions of the agent to write vulnerable code on clean, held-out tasks? We instantiate this attack against three recently proposed self-modifying coding agents: the Darwin Gödel Machine (with our experimental modifications), the Self-Improving Coding Agent, and Hyperagents (both substantively unmodified). We demonstrate successful proofs-of-concept: for example, with Hyperagents powered by Sonnet 4.5, our poisoned benchmark leads the agent to self-evolve instructions that disable HTTPS certificate validation on neutral URL-fetching tasks. From our experiments, we distill properties of the vulnerability, benchmark, model, and agent scaffolding that are sufficient to enable a benchmark poisoning attack. Moreover, we show that contamination often persists even when a poisoned agent is subsequently evolved against clean benchmarks. We discuss defensive directions and argue that self-modifying coding agents must be designed to be more resilient to such attacks.

report.summary: A new arXiv paper shows poisoned benchmarks can make self-modifying AI coding agents evolve insecure behavior, such as disabling HTTPS validation, even on clean tasks.
report.background: Thompson's 1984 essay "Reflections on Trusting Trust" demonstrated that a compiler could be poisoned to reinsert a backdoor into clean source code. Today, AI coding agents increasingly write and improve their own code, using benchmarks to evaluate and evolve future versions. This paper revisits Thompson's attack in that setting: can an adversary poison the benchmarks used by self-modifying agents so that later versions write vulnerable code on clean, held-out tasks? The authors test three systems: the Darwin Gödel Machine with modifications, the Self-Improving Coding Agent, and Hyperagents. They report successful proofs-of-concept, including Hyperagents with Sonnet 4.5 evolving instructions that disable HTTPS certificate validation on neutral URL-fetching tasks. They also find contamination often survives later evolution against clean benchmarks.
key_points: Poisoned benchmarks are a new attack vector: instead of altering model weights or source code, an adversary corrupts the data an agent uses to evaluate and improve itself. The agent then self-evolves harmful instructions, such as disabling HTTPS certificate validation, that generalize to clean tasks.

The attack is not limited to one system. The authors demonstrate it against the Darwin Gödel Machine, Self-Improving Coding Agent, and Hyperagents, with two systems substantively unmodified. They distill properties of the vulnerability, benchmark, model, and agent scaffolding that make such poisoning feasible.

Contamination can persist. When a poisoned agent is later evolved against clean benchmarks, the vulnerability often remains. This suggests that self-modification can bake insecure behavior into an agent's instructions, memory, or scaffolds in ways that are hard to reverse.

The paper argues that self-modifying coding agents need stronger defenses, including benchmark integrity checks, sandboxed self-evaluation, provenance tracking, and adversarial testing. It extends Thompson's classic supply-chain warning to AI systems that rewrite themselves.

The finding matters because coding agents are moving from tools that suggest code to systems that autonomously modify their own code and evaluation loops. If their improvement pipeline is untrusted, a single poisoned benchmark can become a durable backdoor in future agent versions.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes benchmark poisoning as a supply-chain risk for self-improving agents. Companies racing to deploy autonomous coding agents may need to secure evaluation datasets, audit self-modifications, and treat agent scaffolds as critical infrastructure. For developers, the paper warns that using public or third-party benchmarks to fine-tune or evolve agents can silently introduce vulnerabilities like disabled TLS validation, which may then spread into production code. For regular users, the risk is indirect but serious: AI-generated software could inherit hidden weaknesses that are hard to detect and patch. The broader lesson is that trust in AI coding agents cannot rest on clean source alone, because the improvement process itself is an attack surface.
report.tools: To follow this work, watch the Darwin Gödel Machine, Self-Improving Coding Agent, and Hyperagents repositories and papers. Related evaluation and sandboxing tools include SWE-bench, METR's task suites, Inspect AI, OpenAI Evals, Docker/gVisor sandboxes, and supply-chain scanners like Sigstore and SLSA. These can help teams test self-modifying agents, verify benchmark integrity, and constrain what evolved code is allowed to do.
